source: isostyle speculative layers (data/isostyle/METHODS.md): not evidence where confidence > 0

layers.name: Cereal grain
layers.note: Charred grain of wheat or barley. In SW Asia before about 8500 BCE this includes cultivated or gathered wild-type cereals. Recovery depends on flotation, which was rare before the 1970s.

layers.name: Domestic livestock
layers.note: Domestic cattle, sheep, goat or pig. Absent means at least 50 identified specimens (or 8 taxa) with no livestock genus of domestic or uncertain status.

layers.name: Enclosures
layers.note: Ditched enclosures: causewayed camps, rondels, henges. Rondels are dated as a class to 4850–4500 BCE.

layers.name: Megalithic tombs
layers.note: Dolmens, passage and gallery graves, court and portal tombs, chambered cairns and long barrows.

layers.name: Pile dwellings
layers.note: Lake and wetland settlements on piles. Most are dendro-dated, which this layer does not yet use; only radiocarbon-dated ones appear.

layers.name: Houses
layers.note: Dated sites recorded as houses or longhouses. Most excavated houses are filed as plain settlements, so this undercounts heavily.

layers.name: Metallurgy
layers.note: Smelting sites, slag and crucibles. Before 3000 BCE this is mostly the Balkans and Anatolia.

layers.name: Waterlogged organics
layers.note: Dugouts, paddles, bows, fish weirs and traps, trackways, nets and textiles. They survive only in wet ground, so this maps preservation as much as use.

layers.name: Cereal pollen in cores
layers.note: Cerealia-type pollen (Triticum, Hordeum, Avena, Secale types) in lake and bog cores. Pollen travels a few kilometres, not a site. Some wild grasses fall in these types, and SW Asia has wild cereals, so cereal pollen there before farming is natural vegetation, not cultivation. Before farming about 6% of counted levels in Europe already have cereal-type grains, from large wild grasses.

layers.name: Dung-fungus spores in cores
layers.note: Sporormiella, Sordaria, Cercophora and Podospora spores, which grow on herbivore dung. Only cores that count non-pollen palynomorphs; wild herbivores produce them too.

layers.name: Open land (pollen-based)
layers.note: Share of open land (grassland, heath, crops) in each 1° cell, reconstructed from 1,128 pollen records with the REVEALS model. Natural steppe and alpine land count as open too, so read change through time, not the level. Covers 30–75°N, 25°W–50°E only.

layers.name: Ancient genomes
layers.note: Where dated, quality-passing ancient genomes come from. Read the evidence map: it is the denominator for every haplogroup layer.

layers.name: Y: I2
layers.note: Mainly western European hunter-gatherers; persists among early farmers.

layers.name: Y: G2a
layers.note: The commonest Y lineage of the first farmers from Anatolia.

layers.name: Y: R1b
layers.note: Before 3500 BCE rare (some hunter-gatherers); spreads with steppe ancestry after 3000 BCE.

layers.name: Y: R1a
layers.note: Eastern hunter-gatherers; later the Corded Ware expansion.

layers.name: Y: C
layers.note: Old European and Near Eastern hunter-gatherer lineage.

layers.name: Y: J2
layers.note: Caucasus and Near Eastern farmers.

layers.name: Y: H2
layers.note: A rare early-farmer lineage.

layers.name: Y: other
layers.note: Every other Y lineage (E, F, H1, I1, J1, Q, T and unresolved calls).

layers.name: mt: U5
layers.note: The dominant maternal lineage of European hunter-gatherers.

layers.name: mt: U4
layers.note: Eastern and Scandinavian hunter-gatherers.

layers.name: mt: H
layers.note: Common among farmers; the most common lineage in Europe today.

layers.name: mt: K
layers.note: Frequent among early farmers.

layers.name: mt: J
layers.note: Early farmers.

layers.name: mt: T2
layers.note: Early farmers.

layers.name: mt: N1a
layers.note: Characteristic of the LBK, rare later.

layers.name: mt: other
layers.note: Every other mitochondrial lineage, including U2 and X.
